common_name: AU-Cropper Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Cropper was selected by Auburn University specifically for the heat and humidity of the Deep South and bears young, but still needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Cropper is a Chinese chestnut selection released through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program, developed specifically for reliable, precocious production under the heat, humidity, and disease pressure typical of Alabama and the broader Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and begins bearing meaningful crops within a few years of planting rather than the decade or more required by seedling trees. Nuts drop free of the spiny burr at maturity in September–October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy and to maintain the air circulation that helps limit fungal disease pressure in humid Southern summers, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — Chestnut Growers Information
Chestnut Growers of America variety notes
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Chinese Chestnut Cultivar Trials

common_name: AU-Homestead Chestnut (Auburn University Southeastern Chinese Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Homestead was released by Auburn University alongside AU-Cropper as part of the same Southeastern-adapted chestnut breeding effort, and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for full cross-pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Homestead is a Chinese chestnut cultivar developed through Auburn University's chestnut improvement program as a companion release to AU-Cropper, selected for good nut quality and disease tolerance under the heat, humidity, and soil conditions typical of Alabama and the wider Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it inherits strong resistance to chestnut blight, the introduced fungal disease that historically devastated American chestnut, and begins cropping within a few years of planting on a grafted tree. Space trees widely to accommodate the broad, spreading mature canopy typical of Chinese chestnut, and interplant with a second, unrelated named cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts require cross-pollination for a full nut set. Harvest nuts from the ground in September–October as burrs split and drop, and store cured nuts refrigerated for the sweetest flavor, since chestnut starches convert to sugar during cold storage.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — Chestnut Growers Information
Chestnut Growers of America variety notes
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Chinese Chestnut Cultivar Trials

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Allegheny is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars and sets its best crops when planted with Susquehanna, Shenandoah, or another genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to more sun as the tree matures; Allegheny is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars selected by pawpaw breeder Neal Peterson from decades of evaluation work aimed at identifying the largest, best-flavored, and most productive pawpaw seedlings for named release. It produces good-sized fruit with the rich, complex banana-mango-custard flavor pawpaw enthusiasts prize, on a vigorous, dependable tree. As with all pawpaws, Allegheny is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar such as Susquehanna or Shenandoah planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set — pawpaw flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, so hand-pollinating with a small brush between two open flowers of different cultivars can meaningfully improve yield in a home planting. In zone 9, site trees where they get afternoon shade in the hottest years and expect best performance toward the cooler end of the zone.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Wabash is a vigorous named Peterson Pawpaw cultivar and sets its best crops when planted with Susquehanna, Shenandoah, or another genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Wabash is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected from Neal Peterson's long-running breeding program for its combination of large fruit size and notably vigorous, healthy tree growth. Fruit has the classic rich, tropical pawpaw flavor — often described as a cross between banana, mango, and custard — with good flesh-to-seed ratio. As with all pawpaws, Wabash is self-incompatible and requires a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination; hand-pollinating between two different cultivars' open flowers with a small brush improves fruit set in home gardens where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce. Mulch young trees well and keep soil consistently moist through the first two seasons, since pawpaw's shallow, fleshy root system is intolerant of drought while establishing; mature trees are considerably more drought-tolerant.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Potomac is a named Peterson Pawpaw cultivar valued for consistent productivity and sets its best crops when planted with Susquehanna, Shenandoah, or another genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun at fruiting age; Potomac is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected by breeder Neal Peterson for dependable, heavy production alongside good flavor and size — a combination that has made it a popular choice for growers who prioritize consistent yield in a home or small-orchard planting. The rich, custardy flesh has the classic pawpaw flavor profile reminiscent of banana, mango, and vanilla custard, best eaten fresh once the fruit yields to gentle thumb pressure and has developed full aroma. As with all pawpaws, Potomac is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and full fruit set. Pawpaws thrive as an understory tree when young, so give newly planted trees light shade for the first year or two before they adjust to more direct sun, and provide steady moisture through establishment.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program
